tier_reason: Upgrade C to A: benchmark code is public (lap3dkernel/c++SIMD/lap3dkernel.cpp and lap3dkernel/fortran/lap3dpottest.f90), compilers (GCC 9, icpc 2019, ifort 2019), flags and CPU model (Xeon Gold 6128) are all stated, and the flags are tied to the numbers: commit b1c14d2 (2020-03-12) added the Xeon Gold 6128 rows to lap3dkernel/README together with the icpc/ifort lines in run_all_tests.sh, which use identical -fPIC -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -mkl -qopenmp flags. README rows 4.1 (g++ and icpc), 4.0 (gfortran) and 7.7 (ifort) Gpair/s match the record.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Intel rows: icpc 2019 -fPIC -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -mkl -qopenmp -std=c++17 and ifort 2019 -qopenmp -fPIC -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -mkl (commented lines in lap3dkernel/run_all_tests.sh, added in commit b1c14d2 in the same change as the Xeon Gold 6128 results). GNU rows: g++ (9) -fPIC -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -fopenmp -std=c++17 and gfortran (9) -O3 -fopenmp -funroll-loops -march=native from the same script. No -ffast-math on the GNU side; the Intel compilers use their default -fp-model fast=1. Exact Intel compiler update numbers are not given ('2019').
corrections.caveats: The source makes no Fortran-beats-C++ claim. The 1.88x ratio (7.7 vs 4.1 Gpair/s) is derived from the README table. The README notes say 'Clearly C++ w/ VCL beats others by 2x, and nearly 4x w/ custom rsqrt' (laptop section). The gap appears only with ifort: gfortran (4.0) ties g++ (4.1). Hand-vectorised C++ with VCL beats the Fortran: 6.1 (g++) and 18.3 Gpair/s (g++ with custom double rsqrt). Compared with icpc at identical flags, ifort is still 1.88x faster (derived from page data). Intel compiler versions are given only as '2019', and Intel has since discontinued ifort, so reproducing the result needs a legacy toolchain. One machine, 12 OMP threads, one reported figure per row (20 repetitions inside each run). The C++ README row does not say which plain kernel it reports (target-outer or source-outer loop). The kernels differ slightly in work: the Fortran stores coordinates as an array of structs x(3,n) and multiplies by an extra 1/(4 pi) prefactor, while the C++ uses separate X/Y/Z arrays. Neither plain version is tuned. The plain C++ kernel accumulates into pot[t] through plain pointers with no __restrict, which a C++ programmer can add. The SoA/SIMD Fortran variants added in 2026 reach 8.1 Gpair/s on a Ryzen 5700U, the same as C++ with VCL (8.1). The README results section is unfinished ('... (to finish)').
corrections.why_faster: The source does not say. Inference from the code: the inner loop is a floating-point sum into pot(i) (Fortran) or pot[t] (C++). ifort and icpc both default to -fp-model fast=1, which allows that reduction to be reassociated. Fortran's rule that dummy arguments do not alias lets ifort keep pot(i) in a register and vectorise the source loop with AVX-512 sqrt/divide. In the C++ kernel pot is a plain pointer that may alias the inputs (no __restrict), which is the likely reason icpc stays at 4.1. GCC at -O3 without -ffast-math does not reassociate floating-point sums, so neither gfortran nor g++ vectorises the reduction (4.0 vs 4.1). If this holds, the effect comes from Fortran's aliasing semantics combined with Intel's fast floating-point default, not from better Fortran codegen in general.

notes: Real entry with accurate numbers. I upgraded the tier to A because commit b1c14d2 ties the Intel flags to the Xeon Gold 6128 rows. Main shortcomings for the decision record: the win appears only with ifort and not with gfortran (gfortran ties g++); hand-SIMD C++ (VCL, custom rsqrt) beats the Fortran by up to 2.4x; the source makes no claim and gives no mechanism (why_faster above is an inference); ifort is discontinued.

tier_reason: bin/benchmarks.csv at a963d28 has c,userfunc_mandelbrot 0.076702 and julia 0.052706 ms, and the code (perf.c, perf.jl, Makefile, bin/collect.jl) is public. The suite is the Julia project's own (first-party). The CSV carries no compiler or hardware metadata (versions.csv is absent at that commit), and gcc 7.3.1, Julia 1.0.0 and the i7-3960X come from julialang.org/benchmarks, which did not resolve here and was read only as a search snippet. The win most likely comes from C99 complex-multiply semantics, so it stays at C.

corrections.baseline: C version of userfunc_mandelbrot in the same suite (perf.c at the repo root at commit a963d28, now c/perf.c; C99 double complex). Built with gcc 7.3.1 -std=c99 -O$N for N = 0..3; bin/collect.jl keeps the minimum over all four builds and 5 runs each.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: C: gcc 7.3.1 -std=c99 -O$N for N = 0..3 plus Julia's Make.inc CFLAGS, linked with OpenBLAS and openlibm; bin/collect.jl takes the best time over all levels and runs. No -march=native, no -ffast-math or -fcx-limited-range. Julia v1.0.0 default optimisation (-O2, JIT for the host CPU), compile time excluded. Compiler and Julia versions are from julialang.org/benchmarks (search snippet only).
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-3960X 3.30 GHz, 64 GB DDR3-1600, openSUSE LEAP 15.0, single core (from the julialang.org benchmarks page, seen only as a search snippet because the host did not resolve here)
corrections.caveats: The only clear Julia win of the eight benchmarks: Julia is also nominally ahead on matrix_multiply (0.975 of C time, both call OpenBLAS) and recursion_quicksort (0.997), but those are ties (derived from page data). The data is from the Julia 1.0.0 era (gcc 7.3.1, 2012 CPU) and was added to the repo as 'add original benchmarks.csv data (#65)' in 2022. Current CI results sit on julialang.github.io (blocked here). The source gives no mechanism. Reading the code, the C version multiplies C99 double complex values (z*z+c) without -ffast-math or -fcx-limited-range. GCC then adds a NaN check after each complex multiply, with a __muldc3 recovery call on the slow path, as C99 Annex G requires. Julia's z^2 and Fortran's complex multiply use the plain formula without that check (GCC applies Fortran rules to gfortran). gfortran, which uses the same gcc 7.3.1 backend and the same algorithm, runs in 0.053836 ms, matching Julia's 0.052706 ms (derived from page data). That points to C's complex-arithmetic semantics rather than better Julia codegen. The C build has no -march=native, while Julia JITs for the host CPU; this probably does not matter here because the i7-3960X has no FMA. Both sides allocate the 21x26 result array on each call (C malloc/free, Julia comprehension). The Rust (0.75 of C time) and Go (0.78) rows of the same benchmark also beat C and are not recorded here.
corrections.why_faster: The source does not say. Likely cause (inference from perf.c, perf.jl and GCC's documented complex-arithmetic rules): C99 Annex G semantics make GCC check every double complex multiply for a NaN result and call __muldc3 to recover, because the build has no -fcx-limited-range or -ffast-math. Julia's Complex multiply (z^2 lowers to z*z) is the plain four-multiply formula. gfortran on the same GCC backend, which skips the check under Fortran rules, matches Julia's time. So the gap is a complex-arithmetic semantics difference that one C flag removes, not Julia generating faster code from the same work.

notes: Numbers verified on the pinned benchmarks.csv; tier C kept. Shortcomings for the decision record: first-party suite with data from 2018; hardware and compiler details seen only in a search snippet; the 1.46x win tracks C99 complex-multiply semantics (gfortran on the same GCC ties Julia), so it is not a language codegen win; it is one benchmark of eight.

tier_reason: csv-race result-all.csv lists csv-zero, zsv ('zsc (c)') and lazycsv (C++) on all 10 files, and every quoted number matches. The harness code is public (src/zig/src/csv_zero.zig, src/c/zsv/main.c and build.sh, src/cpp/lazycsv/main.cpp and build.sh, generate_charts.py with poop), the flags are stated (zig --release=fast, cc -O3, g++ -std=c++17 -O3 -march=native) and so is the CPU (Ryzen 5 PRO 5650U). A holds through the lazycsv baseline. libzsv's own build flags and the cc/g++ versions are not stated.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: csv-race at the Dec 2025 results commit: Zig 0.15.2 'zig build --release=fast' (build.zig uses standardTargetOptions, so the default target is the native CPU); zsv harness 'cc -O3 main.c -lzsv' against a manually built, system-installed libzsv whose flags are not stated; lazycsv 'g++ -std=c++17 -O3 -march=native'; Rust 'cargo build --release'. The cc and g++ versions are not stated. Timed with poop -d 10000 (perf counters). The harness moved to Zig 0.16 (May 2026) after the results were taken.
corrections.claimed_speedup: csv-race result-all.csv wall times, csv-zero vs zsv (C) vs lazycsv (C++): ~32 MB no-quotes 52 col 6.62 ms vs 14.1 ms vs 18.7 ms; ~696 MB 574 ms vs 1.50 s vs 1.25 s; ~3.2 GB no-quotes 603 ms vs 1.32 s vs 1.65 s (Rust simd-csv 870 ms); ~9.9 GB quoted 7.73 s vs 12.7 s vs 12.1 s. csv-zero is the fastest of the 5 parsers on all 10 files. Ratios are 1.36x to 2.61x against zsv and 1.08x to 2.85x against lazycsv (derived from page data). On the four real-world files csv-zero takes 0.78 to 2.86 ms (775 us on nfl.csv vs zsv 1.78 ms). These files are only 0.72 to 2.6 MB, so the rows include process start-up (the ~1 KB file takes 427 us). Independent corroboration: LangArena results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js (AMD Ryzen 7 3800X), CSV::Parse runtime: Zig 0.974 s, best C row C/Clang 2.223 s, C++/Clang++ 2.348 s. The Zig implementation imports csv-zero (zig/build.zig.zon). Rust (0.881 s) and Zig/Unchecked (0.585 s) are faster still.
corrections.caveats: The harness is written by the csv-zero author, and the task only counts fields, so it isolates scanning and says nothing about downstream parsing. No harness step checks that the parsers report the same field count. The result chart set shows the top five parsers only; result-all.csv holds the five measured here (csv-parser, rapidcsv, csv-core and a Go parser are built by the Makefile but not in the CSV). 'zsc (c)' is the zsv library linked with -lzsv from a manual build whose flags are not stated, and its harness is built without -march=native. lazycsv and csv-zero (native Zig target) both target the host CPU. lazycsv memory-maps the input (10.6 GB peak RSS on the 9.9 GB file) instead of using a 64 KB buffer. The four real-world files are 0.72-2.6 MB samples (nfl 1.36 MB, worldcitiespop 0.96 MB, mbta 0.72 MB, game 2.6 MB), so those rows partly measure process start-up. The results date from 2025-12-22/23. Later harness changes: a Zig 0.16 pin, and a fix by the simd-csv author (2026-07-30) that removed double buffering in the Rust csv and simd-csv harnesses, so those two Rust rows are understated. csv-zero's CRLF chunk-boundary fix (2026-01-06) does not affect these LF-only files. Single machine (laptop-class Ryzen 5 PRO 5650U), one table. The csv-zero README claims it outperforms every library in csv-race but gives no numbers; the numbers come from result-all.csv. In LangArena the C/C++ CSV implementations were not inspected, and Rust beats the Zig row there. zsv (C) is already catalogued as a separate entry; this record is about the Zig library.

notes: Accurate record; tier A kept on the strength of the lazycsv (-O3 -march=native) comparison. Shortcomings for the decision record: the author's own harness; libzsv build flags and C/C++ compiler versions are unstated; the task only counts fields, with no cross-check of counts; small real-world files are start-up dominated; the harness changed after the results; LangArena's 2026-10-05 run independently confirms Zig (csv-zero) 0.974 s vs C/Clang 2.223 s.
